'''Katrina T. Forest''' (born 1966) is an American biologist who is the EB Fred Professor of Bacteriology and Chair in the Department of Bacteriology at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]]. Her research considers the use of [[structural biology]] to better understand [[pathogenesis]]. Forest is a Fellow of the [[American Society for Microbiology]].

== Early life and education ==
Forest was born in [[Honolulu]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Pfahler|first=Sandy|date=2007-04-30|title=Oral History Interview: Katrina Forest (864)|url=https://minds.wisconsin.edu/handle/1793/73728|language=en}}</ref> Her father was in the [[United States Navy]], and she lived in [[Philadelphia]], [[Baltimore]] and [[Madison, Wisconsin|Madison]] during her childhood. She was encouraged to study science at university, and eventually completed her bachelor's degree at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Citation|last=McMahon|first=Katherine|chapter=Katrina T. Forest: A Renaissance Woman in Microbiology|date=2018|chapter-url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1128/9781555819545.ch12|title=Women in Microbiology|pages=105–111|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd|language=en|doi=10.1128/9781555819545.ch12|isbn=978-1-68367-057-5|access-date=2021-03-20|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> Her mother became unwell whilst she was an undergraduate student, and Forest spent a semester closer to home at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref name=":0" /> She moved to [[Princeton University]] for her doctoral research, where she used [[x-ray crystallography]] to understand [[pertussis toxin]].<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=X-ray and electron crystallography applied to pertussis toxin|date=1993|language=English|first=Katrina T|last=Forest|oclc=28518422 }}</ref> Forest was a postdoctoral researcher at [[Scripps Research]] where she specialized in protein crystallography.<ref name=":0" />

== Research and career ==
Forest was appointed to the faculty at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in 1998. She was promoted to Professor in 2009.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=UW Bacteriology {{!}} People|url=https://bact.wisc.edu/people_profile.php?t=rf&p=kforres1|access-date=2021-03-20|website=bact.wisc.edu}}</ref> She was the first to realize the three-dimensional structures of a bacterial [[phytochrome]], and predicted that the bacteriophytochrome architecture first arose around one billion years ago. The phytochrome tells plants when to germinate and when not to germinate, as well as identifying where plants should grow to absorb the most light possible.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Scientists map one of biology's critical light-sensing structures|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2005-11/uow-smo111405.php|access-date=2021-03-20|website=EurekAlert!|language=en}}</ref> She derived the phytochrome from ''[[Deinococcus radiodurans]]'', a species of bacterium that was known to be tolerant to ionising radiation.<ref name=":2" /> The phytochrome was isolated, crystallized and investigated using [[x-ray crystallography]].<ref name=":2" /> Forest identified that the protein had a knot, which she predicts may serve to stabilize the protein so that it can capture sunlight.<ref name=":2" /> In the absence of such a structure, Forest believes that the phytochrome would undergo a conformational change under illumination, and wouldn't be able to effectively capture the sunlight.<ref name=":2" /> Such structures can store the light they absorb for several days, which allows the plant to predict where the light may come from each day.<ref name=":2" /> Forest went on to study the light-harvesting mechanisms of [[Actinomycetota|actinobacteria]], identifying two light-capturing molecular components that absorb light at different energies.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-10-11|title=We [Heart] Actinobacteria|url=https://www.marinetechnologynews.com/news/heart-actinobacteria-539788|access-date=2021-03-20|website=Marine Technology News|language=en}}</ref>

Recognizing the impact of protein molecular structure on biological function, Forest turned to the design of novel proteins with tuneable properties.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Scientists create super-strong collagen|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/01/100112135040.htm|access-date=2021-03-20|website=ScienceDaily|language=en}}</ref> Amongst these, she identified a stable synthetic [[collagen]] that may offer hope for conditions such as arthritis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shoulders|first1=Matthew D.|last2=Satyshur|first2=Kenneth A.|last3=Forest|first3=Katrina T.|last4=Raines|first4=Ronald T.|date=2010-01-12|title=Stereoelectronic and steric effects in side chains preorganize a protein main chain|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=107|issue=2|pages=559–564|doi=10.1073/pnas.0909592107|issn=0027-8424|pmid=20080719|pmc=2818912 |bibcode=2010PNAS..107..559S |doi-access=free}}</ref> The modified protein contains less flexible amino acids to the original form, which stiffens the structure and helps the protein to maintain structural integrity even when exposed to elevated temperatures.<ref>{{Cite web|last=ghesselberg@madison.com {{!}} 608-252-6140|first=GEORGE HESSELBERG {{!}}|title=UW-Madison team's collagen find could help treat arthritis|url=https://madison.com/news/local/education/university/uw-madison-teams-collagen-find-could-help-treat-arthritis/article_5f33cfc4-24fe-5a7a-b533-9dd28a1a0ca0.html|access-date=2021-03-20|website=madison.com|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Scientists Create Super-Strong Collagen|url=https://www.newswise.com/articles/uw-madison-scientists-create-super-strong-collagen|access-date=2021-03-20|website=www.newswise.com|language=en}}</ref>

Forest worked with [[Laura L. Kiessling]] to investigate the protein [[Intelectin]], demonstrating that it can identify different types of pathogens and distinguish pathogens from human cells.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Protein Suggests a New Strategy to Thwart Infection|url=https://news.wisc.edu/protein-suggests-a-new-strategy-to-thwart-infection/|access-date=2021-03-20|website=news.wisc.edu|language=en-US}}</ref> The pair showed that this protein is [[upregulate]]d during infection, indicating that it might have some antimicrobial properties.<ref name=":3" />

Alongside her work on proteins, Forest has studied [[Type IV pili]] (T4P), [[organelle]]s that mediate the attachment of bacteria to one another. Forest has investigated the mechanisms and dynamics of the pilus proteins that make up T4P.<ref name=":1" />
